18 months is enough to have a real read.

title: OpenAI rejection after full loop
OpenAI close call
content:
OpenAI close call

**Result:** Pending
**Number of Rounds:** 5

Phone screen was KV store serialization. Parts 1 through 3: basic serialization, file splitting with size limit, then append-only log variant. Got through all three.

VO was 5 rounds. GPU Credits for coding round 1, went fine. Coding round 2 was the virus transmission simulation with immunity states. Part 1 basic, part 2 adds the X state with duration tracking and state transition logic. More edge cases than expected.

System design was DevBox (IDE environment). Interviewer had built it. Went deep on scalability and storage, but there were domain-specific areas I couldn't match their depth on.

Deep dive was fine. Behavioral included "what if AI causes unemployment" which I wasn't expecting.

Recruiter said "close call" and flagged me for a sooner reinterview, possibly 6 months out. No rejection email. Still parsing what that means.

title: 7 months at Anthropic
content:
Anthropic - Company Culture - Software Engineer

**Time at Company:** 7 months

Took the job for the mission. Seven months in, the mission is real. The work is meaningful and people genuinely believe in what they're building.

What they don't advertise is the constant performance pressure dressed up as purpose. Everyone here is brilliant, and the implicit comparison never goes away. Meetings are intellectually exhausting in a way that doesn't always feel productive.

Pay is competitive. But don't join expecting to coast on competence. You won't.

title: Anthropic - Company Culture - Software Engineer
content:
Anthropic - Company Culture - Software Engineer

**Time at Company:** 1.5 years

Joined thinking it would be the most meaningful work of my career. Working on AI safety, surrounded by sharp people with a real mission. And some of that is actually true.

The problems are genuinely hard and the mission doesn't feel hollow. That part landed.

But there's a real "are you one of us" thing here that doesn't go away after you're hired. Got passed over for a project I'd been building toward for months. Reason given was vague. Talked to others who've been here longer with the same experience.

WLB is fine on paper. In practice the expectations are high and unstated. Nobody tells you to work weekends. You just feel it.

The culture round filters for a very specific type, and that filter applies internally too. If you care about the mission, it's worth it. If you need to know where you stand and why, this isn't the place.

title: Anthropic makes you code without AI assist, but they build the AI coding tool
content: Something that stood out after my Anthropic phone screen and onsite: no autocomplete, no AI assistance anywhere in the loop. You're on CodeSignal in a bare notebook, timed, just you and the libraries. Meanwhile the company's flagship product is Claude Code. Nobody explains it, and none of the interviewers seemed bothered either. The bar isn't algorithms, it's knowing stuff like PIL or concurrency primitives cold, which honestly feels kinda weird to gate hiring on in 2026. Would've avoided this format if I had the choice, but there wasn't one.

title: Anthropic - Company Culture - Research Engineer
content:
Anthropic - Company Culture - Research Engineer

**Time at Company:** 14 months

WLB: team-dependent. Research teams push harder around model releases. Not 24/7 but crunch is real.

Management: strong at the IC level. Above that it gets less clear.

Mission: genuinely real. Internal safety focus isn't branding, people actually argue about it.

Comp: strong base. Equity is a private company bet. One refresh in my tenure.

Culture: high individual bar. Smart people. Low tolerance for coasting.

Watch out for: ambiguity. Scope isn't handed to you. If you need clear ownership defined from day one, this isn't the fit.

Good for: frontier problems, high autonomy, you're comfortable figuring out what matters.

Not good for: people who need predictable structure or a defined playbook.

title: Anthropic 5 rounds done - culture is the wild card
Got OpenAI offer
content:
OpenAI - Interview Experience - Software Engineer

**Result:** Offer
**Number of Rounds:** 5

Not bragging or anything, but wasn't expecting to make it through all 5 rounds.

Phone screen was SD + coding. Problem description was long but the core wasn't that bad once you stripped it down. Passed first try.

Onsite had GPU Credits as the first coding round, a payment system SD, BQ, and a deep dive. Deep dive was the most personal one. Went through my last two projects in detail. Interviewer clearly read my resume before the call, which was a nice change from some other onsites I've had.

Fifth round was a values conversation. They care a lot about the mission stuff and you can tell pretty quickly if your answers are genuine or canned. I came in with a real perspective.

Got the offer about a week later. Process was surprisingly smooth.

title: Anthropic - Company Culture - Software Engineer
content:
Anthropic - Company Culture - Software Engineer

**Time at Company:** 8 months

Eight months in and still feel like I got lucky landing here. The mission stuff isn't just marketing, you actually feel it in what gets prioritized day to day.

Work is intense but teammates are sharp and genuinely collaborative. Haven't seen the credit-hoarding politics I dealt with at my last company.

The ambiguity is real though. Priorities shift and you have to self-direct a lot. If you need clear structure this probably isn't the fit, but if you're okay figuring things out it's great.
